To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mean prey weight of carnivores increases with predator weight, that the range of prey size increases with predator weight and that the ratio of prey size to predator size decreases with predator weight.
(1), the size of prey taken by a predator is positively correlated with predator body mass, and (2) this relationship is best described by a log-normal distribution of prey sizes in predator rations.

(a) the ratio of prey to predator weight tends toward a constant for predators that are specialized carnivores, (b) insectivores take prey of a much smaller size relative to themselves and (c) the upper limit of predator biomass is independent, of predator weight.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between predator and prey body size.
the relationship between prey size and predator size in the context of food web structure and dynamics.
the relation between predator and prey in the terrestrial food chain and the implications for the structure of food chains and the dynamics of predator populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prey size taken by a predator is determined by the predator's size, its trophic specialization, its prey's availability, its foraging efficiency, and the predator's own energy requirements.
the size of prey taken by predators tends to decrease with predator size, but that the relationship between predator and prey weight is not linear and varies among trophic specialiations.
the size and abundance of prey are the most important determinants of the size, structure and abundance of terrestrial vertebrate predator populations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the trophic level of a species is determined by both its body size and its diet, while the biomass at a trophic level is a function of the biomass of the trophic levels immediately below it.
the size of the predator is the primary determinant of prey size, and that the size of prey taken is an inverse function of predator size.

(1), the food web is more complex than previously believed, (2) there is a general tendency for the mean prey size to decline relative to the size of the predator as the predator becomes larger and (3) there is a tendency for larger predators to feed on a wider range of prey sizes than do smaller ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a strong correlation between predator and prey sizes, and that this correlation can be described with a set of simple equations.
the size of prey taken by terrestrial vertebrate predators varies systematically with the size of their predators.
the size of the prey taken by terrestrial vertebrate predators is a function of predator size.
